meta.titre: Summarise the general lesson or message conveyed by a reading passage

sections.contenu_markdown: The final question of a comprehension exercise often asks not for a fact, but for the STORY'S POINT - the one idea the writer wants a reader to take away. Answering it well means stepping back from the details to see the bigger picture.

items: Identifying the main character's situation at the beginning and at the end of a passage
Distinguishing a specific detail from a general, transferable idea

sections.titre: Summarising the lesson of a passage
sections.contenu_markdown:
A "lesson" or "message" question asks the reader to generalise beyond the specific events of the passage: what broader idea, applicable beyond this one story, does the passage illustrate? To answer well, compare the situation at the START of the passage with the situation at the END, and identify what CHANGED and WHY - this change usually points directly to the lesson.

The answer should be phrased as a general statement ("one should...", "this shows that..."), not simply a repetition of what happened to the specific character, and it must remain clearly connected to the passage's actual content, not be an unrelated generic saying.
sections.formule_principale: \text{Lesson} = \text{generalise the change (start} \to \text{end) beyond the specific character}

sections.enonce_markdown: A passage tells of a farmer who initially refused to try a new irrigation method suggested by an agricultural officer, then eventually tried it after a poor harvest, and doubled his yield the following year. What lesson can be drawn from this passage?

etapes.action: Identify the situation at the start
etapes.justification: The starting point establishes what attitude or behaviour will change.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Start: the farmer refuses to try a new method, sticking to old habits

etapes.action: Identify the situation at the end and what caused the change
etapes.justification: The ending shows the result of a changed attitude, caused by a specific event (the poor harvest).
etapes.resultat_markdown: End: after a poor harvest, he tries the new method and doubles his yield

etapes.action: Generalise this change into a broader lesson
etapes.justification: The lesson should apply beyond just this one farmer's specific situation.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Being open to new ideas or methods, even when unfamiliar, can lead to significant improvement

sections.conclusion_markdown: The lesson is that remaining open-minded and willing to try new approaches, rather than clinging only to familiar habits, can bring real benefits - a general idea illustrated by, but not limited to, this particular farmer's experience.

items.erreur_markdown: Simply retelling what happened to the character ("the farmer tried a new method and got a better harvest") instead of stating the general lesson.
items.pourquoi_faux: A summary of events is not the same as a LESSON: the question asks for the broader, transferable idea that the story illustrates, not merely a restatement of the plot.
items.correction_markdown: Always phrase the final answer as a general statement (applicable to readers in general), not as a recap of what specifically happened to the character.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving a generic, well-known saying unrelated to the actual content of the passage (e.g. "hard work always pays off" for a passage that was really about honesty).
items.pourquoi_faux: The lesson must be clearly grounded in what actually happens in THIS particular passage; a generic moral that could apply to almost any story, without any real connection to its specific content, does not demonstrate genuine understanding of the text.
items.correction_markdown: Before finalising an answer, check that the proposed lesson is specifically supported by the events and change described in this passage, not just a generic saying loosely applied.

items.enonce_markdown: A passage describes a student who cheated on a test, was caught, and lost the trust of her teacher for the rest of the year. What is the most likely lesson of this passage?
items.solution_markdown: Dishonesty may bring a short-term advantage but can cause lasting damage to one's reputation and relationships once discovered.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain, in general terms, why comparing the BEGINNING and the END of a passage is a reliable method for identifying its lesson.
items.solution_markdown: The lesson of a passage is almost always revealed through some kind of CHANGE experienced by the main character (a change in attitude, behaviour, or circumstances). Comparing the starting situation to the ending situation makes this change explicit and easy to identify, and the REASON for that change (what caused it) usually points directly to the general idea or message the writer intends to convey - making this comparison a reliable, systematic method rather than a vague guess.

items.enonce_markdown: A passage describes two neighbours: one who always shares his harvest with others in the village and is helped by them during a difficult period, and another who keeps everything to himself and receives no help when he later faces the same difficulty. Propose a well-supported lesson for this passage, explaining how each detail supports it.
items.solution_markdown: The lesson is that generosity towards others is often reciprocated when one is in need, while selfishness can leave a person isolated at the moment they most need support. This is supported by the clear contrast the passage draws between the two neighbours: the generous one receives help during hardship (a direct consequence of his earlier sharing), while the selfish one, having never shared, receives no such support when he later faces a similar hardship - the parallel structure of the passage (two neighbours, same type of difficulty, opposite outcomes) makes this contrast, and the lesson it illustrates, deliberate and explicit rather than coincidental.

items_markdown: A 'lesson' question asks for a general, transferable idea, not a retelling of the specific events.
Compare the situation at the start and at the end of the passage to identify the key change and its cause.
Phrase the answer as a general statement, clearly grounded in the passage's actual content.
Avoid generic sayings that could apply to any story without a real, specific connection to this passage.
